chapter_title: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
learning_objective: The learner will differentiate reinforcing loops, in which a prediction helps bring itself about, from balancing loops, in which a prediction helps prevent itself, by labeling the direction of every link in three prediction loops and classifying each loop, with at least 9 of 10 links and all 3 loops correct.
specification:
Type: causal-loop **sim-id:** prediction-feedback-loops
**Library:** vis-network
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** differentiate
**Learning Objective:** The learner will differentiate reinforcing loops, in which a prediction helps bring itself about, from balancing loops, in which a prediction helps prevent itself, by labeling the direction of every link in three prediction loops and classifying each loop, with at least 9 of 10 links and all 3 loops correct. **Prerequisites:** predictive model, data bias (measurement bias), self-fulfilling prophecy, self-defeating prophecy, student risk prediction, predictive policing (defined in Parts One and Four above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner labels each of the 10 links as "same direction" (+) or "opposite direction" (−), then classifies each of the 3 loops as reinforcing or balancing, then answers one question per loop. A label, classification or answer is correct when it matches the Content tables. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 links, 3 of 3 loops and 2 of 3 loop questions correct on the first attempt. Opening a node's explanation is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A loop with a minus sign in it must be balancing (Loop 2 has two minus signs and is reinforcing). (2) A prediction that comes true proves the model was accurate (Loop 1). (3) A forecast that "failed" was a bad forecast (Loop 3). (4) Taking more data from the same source fixes a feedback loop (Loop 1 question). **Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level work means taking a loop apart into its links and finding the structure that decides its behavior. Labeling each link before classifying the loop makes the learner derive the loop type from the parts, using the counting rule, rather than guessing from the story's moral. **Content:** Definitions shown to the learner: - Same direction (+): if the first factor rises, the second rises; if the first falls, the second falls. - Opposite direction (−): if the first factor rises, the second falls; if the first falls, the second rises. - Reinforcing loop: a change travels around the loop and comes back larger, in the same direction. A self-fulfilling prediction is a reinforcing loop. - Balancing loop: a change travels around the loop and comes back opposed. A self-defeating prediction is a balancing loop. - Counting rule: a loop with an even number of opposite (−) links, including zero, is reinforcing; a loop with an odd number is balancing. to a still higher risk score. | | 3 | L8, L9, L10 | 1 | Balancing | One opposite link: a forecast of heavy traffic leads to lighter traffic and a lower forecast next week, so the prediction defeats itself. | Outside factor shown in Loop 1 but not part of the loop: "True crime in the district," with a + link to "Crimes recorded in that district." Its note reads: "Records rise with true crime and with patrols; the model cannot tell which." Loop questions (one per loop, three choices each): | # | Question | Choices | Correct | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---| | Q1 | Which change would weaken Loop 1? | Train the model on crimes reported by victims and residents rather than on crimes discovered by patrols; send more patrols to every district; retrain the model every week instead of every month | Train on reported crimes | Records that do not depend on where the patrols went no longer carry L2's effect into L3; more patrols or more frequent retraining only feed the same loop. | | Q2 | Which use of the risk score would turn Loop 2 from harm to help? | Keep the student in the challenging course and add tutoring when the score is high; hide the score from the student; recompute the score every month | Keep the course and add tutoring | Adding support instead of lowering the placement replaces link L5's loss of challenging work with more help, so a high score leads to higher grades. | | Q3 | Next Sunday the 9 AM forecast said "heavy traffic," and the road was light. What is the best explanation? | Drivers acted on the forecast, so the jam it predicted did not form; the model was badly trained; traffic is purely random | Drivers acted on the forecast | In a balancing loop a useful forecast can look wrong, because people change their behavior to avoid what it predicts. | **Provenance:** The loops are simplified from the chapter sections "Self-Fulfilling Prophecy," "Student Risk Prediction," and "Predictive Policing." The link directions are the chapter's qualitative claims, not measured effects; the sim labels the diagram "Simplified causal model: directions only, no sizes." **Rules:** - Links are labeled one at a time in the order L1 to L10 (fixed). Each link has one scored attempt; after it, the correct label and Why text are shown and the link displays its correct sign. - A loop can be classified only after all of its links are labeled. Each loop has one scored attempt. - The loop questions are answered after all three loops are classified, in the order Q1, Q2, Q3, one scored attempt each. - Scoring: links 0 to 10, loops 0 to 3, questions 0 to 3. Mastery requires links >= 9, loops = 3 and questions >= 2. - The counting rule is shown only after the learner's first loop classification, whether right or wrong. - Start Over resets every label, classification, answer and score. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the definitions of same-direction and opposite-direction links and sees Loop 1 with its three links unlabeled. 2. The learner labels L1, L2 and L3; after each, the feedback appears and the sign is drawn on the link. 3. The learner classifies Loop 1 as reinforcing or balancing; the feedback and the counting rule appear. 4. The learner repeats steps 2 and 3 for Loop 2 (L4 to L7) and Loop 3 (L8 to L10). 5. The learner answers Q1, Q2 and Q3. 6. The learner should notice that Loop 2 contains two opposite links and still reinforces, and that the loop which looks like a failed forecast, Loop 3, is the one in which the forecast worked. **Feedback:** Correct link: "Correct:" plus the Why text. Incorrect link: "This link runs the [same/opposite] way:" plus the Why text. Correct loop: "Correct:" plus the Why text. Incorrect loop: "Count the opposite links: [n]. This loop is [classification]:" plus the Why text. Questions: "Correct:" or "The best answer is: [choice].", plus the Why text. Running scores "Links n of 10, Loops n of 3, Questions n of 3" are shown throughout. At the end, if mastery is met: "You can read a feedback loop: a prediction about people can make itself come true, or keep itself from coming true."; otherwise: "Look again at Loop 2: count its opposite links before deciding." **Starting State:** Loop 1 is shown with its three nodes, the outside factor, and three unlabeled links. The question on screen is "If the model predicts more crime here, what happens next?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter describes the predictive policing loop (patrols where crime is predicted, more crime discovered, more records, higher prediction), the student risk loop (a high-risk label leading to a less demanding class, lower learning and a higher score), and a self-defeating traffic forecast for 9 AM on the road to Delphi. It names Merton (1948) and the Lum and Isaac Oakland study (2016), which the sim does not need to show.
